## Spatial Predictive Modeling of Residential Burglary Using 311 Service Request Data (Garbage Cans) in Chicago

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Introduction

With the "Broken Windows Theory" in mind, the goal of this assignment is to critically analyze predictive policing models. This theory, according to lecutre diuscussions, is the idea that visible signs of social disorder are some indication of crime. Specifically, my assignment used 311 data where residents reported missing or stolen garbage cans as a predictor in determining burglaries in Chicago. The aim of this report is not only to create a predicitve model in which if we can find where missing garbage cans are concnetrated, we predict where burglaries will occur, but also to crtically evaluate the model and data sources.

This report outlines the various spatial operations conducted above, outlining what the code is for (in general), and why it is needed to meet the overall goal of the assignment. As the coding and spatial operations apporach sections with results, those results will be interpreted through out these code and operational debriefings. Finally, the report will conclude a ciritcal evaluation of the findings in this analysis.


::: {.cell}

Prior to creating any fishnet or spatial operations, the report wanted a baseline map, specfically two maps adjacent to one another to see where missing garbage cart complaints were concentrated. The first map, the one the left, or A in the code, uses red dots across Chicago, whereas the map, B, is a smoothed out desnity map showing the concentrations. The second map is created using Kernal Density Estimation. That is, KDE uses some mathematical formula to to show hotspots. The kernel is the center of the se maps. In my code, I opted for 10 bins, which is essentially the number of density level.

In any spatial analysis it is critical to explore and visualize the data we are working with, and thus we need to understand our original data before we can even begin using it as predictors. In the maps below, we can see that the first map, A, there were almost 53k complaints and a lot of it was concentrated everywhere with noticeable gaps in some southern parts and what looks like along the river and in the eastern parts of the city. Though I am not familiar with Chicago's landscape, this pattern may exists for numerous reason, such as less residents in those areas, or just lack of need for complaints such as those. Further, the second map on the right, B, illustrates the same patter, by showing that colours in purple, which are lesser concentrated areas, are in the same places mentioned earlier. Besides these areas, it looks like garbage complaints exist across the city and dont seep to have specific neighbourhoods of concern. That said, there are very obvious hotspots on map B, where there may be spatial patterns and thus the need for more modeling.

#### Fishnet Grid Creation

By creating a fishnet, we are essentially converting the point data from above to a grid format where we can count the points per grid or cell. From there we can calculate spatial features and then actually run regression as done below. It's importatnt to note that fishnets adress MAUP concerns, albeit selecting the right size is a challenge in and if itself. Nonetheless, the consistent cell size allows us to make more reliable comparisons across Chicago.

The below out put shows how mnay cells cover Chicgo, in this case it is nearly 2500, which also acts as the number of observations in our data. Each cell is exactly 250,000 sq meters.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#CREATING THE FISHNET

fishnet <- st_make_grid(
  chicagoBoundary,
  cellsize = 500,
  square = TRUE
) %>%
  st_sf() %>%
  mutate(uniqueID = row_number()) %>%
  st_transform('ESRI:102271')

# Keeping only cells inside Chicago
fishnet <- fishnet[chicagoBoundary, ]


cat("✓ Created fishnet grid\n")
```

When looking at the fishnet summary output for burglaries, we can see it also ranges from zero, but only to 40 incidents per cell.

#### Part 3: Spatial Features

Keeping this in mind, we also need a baseline for burglaries where the kernal density here is actually simliar to the garbage above, where the south also has gaps. This section essentially uses past burglaries and averages it across a surface using the sigma 1000 code, which is just a 1km bandwidth. The higher the value, the more burgaries have occured in that spot. In addition to this visual inspection, we also use the later on to determine if more complex models we'll build later do any better than this in predicting where burglaries will occur.

The map shows clear strong concentrations in the north and a bit south, closer to the center.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# KDE is calculated on burglaries y
burglaries_ppp <- as.ppp(
  st_coordinates(burglaries),
  W = as.owin(st_bbox(chicagoBoundary))
)

kde_burglaries <- density.ppp(
  burglaries_ppp,
  sigma = 1000,
  edge = TRUE
)

kde_raster <- rast(kde_burglaries)

fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  mutate(
    kde_value = terra::extract(
      kde_raster,
      vect(fishnet),
      fun = mean,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )[, 2]
  )

cat("✓ Calculated KDE baseline\n")
```

```{.r .cell-code}
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "KDE Value",
```

Further to capture more context that may be overlooked by the fishnet count, we also want to look at the average of the nearest 3 fishnets, since its possibel to have cells with more or less counts, but the proximity is important to note. When there is a low value that means there is less distance between garbage cart complaints and cells. Higher values might indicate that a particular cell is further away from complaints. Evidently, the range in the summary table is quite vast from just over 6.3 to almost 2300.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#knn distance-Spatial features
#here we want to see how close each cell is to closest event. if there is no land in a cell, but it is still close to a a bunch or cluster will still get some distance value to capture what the count is missing. 

fishnet_coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(fishnet)) #for each fishnet cell how far is it from the nearest garbage cart complaint. we need a centroid for that cell
garbage_coords  <- st_coordinates(garbagecart) #coords

nn_result <- get.knnx(garbage_coords, fishnet_coords, k = 3)

fishnet <- fishnet %>%
  mutate(garbage.nn = rowMeans(nn_result$nn.dist))

cat("✓ Calculated nearest neighbor distances\n")
```

```{.r .cell-code}
#Local Moran's I

# Function to calculate Local Moran's I
calculate_local_morans <- function(data, variable, k = 5) {
  
  # Create spatial weights
  coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(data))
  neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = k))
  weights <- nb2listw(neighbors, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  
  # Calculate Local Moran's I
 local_moran <- localmoran(as.numeric(data[[variable]]), weights)
  
  # Classify clusters
  mean_val <- mean(data[[variable]], na.rm = TRUE)
  
  data %>%
    mutate(
      local_i = local_moran[, 1],
      p_value = local_moran[, 5],
      is_significant = p_value < 0.05,
      
      moran_class = case_when(
        !is_significant ~ "Not Significant",
        local_i > 0 & .data[[variable]] > mean_val ~ "High-High",
        local_i > 0 & .data[[variable]] <= mean_val ~ "Low-Low",
        local_i < 0 & .data[[variable]] > mean_val ~ "High-Low",
        local_i < 0 & .data[[variable]] <= mean_val ~ "Low-High",
        TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
      )
    )
}

# Apply to missing or stolen garbage carts
fishnet <- calculate_local_morans(fishnet, "countGarbage", k = 5)

nrow(fishnet)
```

#### Part 4: Count Regression Models

To actually predict burglaries, we need a regression model. Since our outcome variable, countBurglaries, is a count rathern than continuous number, regular linear regression isn't appropriate here. Instead, we use count regression, starting with Poisson. The model takes three predictors, countGarbage, garbage.nn, and dist_to_hotspot , and estimates how each one relates to the expected number of burglaries per cell.

However, it is important to note that Poisson regression comes with an important assumption: it assumes that the variance in the data equals the mean. But in reality, crime data likely will not meet this assumption. So, when the variance is much higher than the mean, the data is considered overdispersed and Poisson underestimates uncertainty in the model. To check for this, we calculated the dispersion parameter from the Poisson residuals. Anything 1.5 suggests overdispersion and needs more flexible model. As shown in the output, our dispersion, 3.45,  was well above this confirming that the Negative Binomial model is more appropriate since it adds an extra parameter specifically to handle this.

#### Part 5: Spatial Cross-Validation

One of the most important parts of building any predictive model is testing whether it actually works on data it has not seen before. In other words, is is generalizable? Since in the regular cross validation model randomly split cells, the model could essentially memorize local patterns and appear to perform well without actually generalizing. So, instead, we use Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) spatial cross-validation, which holds out one entire police district at a time. The model trains on all remaining districts and then tries to predict burglaries ion the one left out . This is repeated for every district, giving us a better picture of how the model performs in areas it has never been trained on. The two error metrics we report are MAE (Mean Absolute Error), which tells us on average how many burglaries off our predictions are per cell, and RMSE which penalizes larger errors more heavily. Lower values for both indicate better model performance. Districts with particularly high MAE are worth noting, as those are the places our model struggles with the most, which can point to something about those neighbourhoods that our predictors are not capturing well.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Get unique districts
districts <- unique(fishnet_model$District)
cv_results <- tibble()

cat("Running LOGO Cross-Validation...\n")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Running LOGO Cross-Validation...
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
for (i in seq_along(districts)) {
  
  test_district <- districts[i]
  
  # Split data
  train_data <- fishnet_model %>% filter(District != test_district)
  test_data <- fishnet_model %>% filter(District == test_district)
  
  # Fit model on training data
  model_cv <- glm.nb(
    countBurglaries ~ countGarbage + garbage.nn + 
      dist_to_hotspot,
    data = train_data
  )
  
  # Predict on test data
  test_data <- test_data %>%
    mutate(
      prediction = predict(model_cv, test_data, type = "response")
    )
  
  # Calculate metrics
  mae <- mean(abs(test_data$countBurglaries - test_data$prediction))
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((test_data$countBurglaries - test_data$prediction)^2))
  
  # Store results
  cv_results <- bind_rows(
    cv_results,
    tibble(
      fold = i,
      test_district = test_district,
      n_test = nrow(test_data),
      mae = mae,
      rmse = rmse
    )
  )
  
  cat("  Fold", i, "/", length(districts), "- District", test_district, 
      "- MAE:", round(mae, 2), "\n")
}
```

#### Part 6: Model Evaluation

The final step is to compare our model to the KDE baseline we created earlier. The KDE baseline is essentially the simplest possible prediction: it just smooths past burglary locations and assumes that crime will continue to happen where it happened before, with no other information. For our more complex model to be worth the effort, it has to do better than this simple baseline.

The three maps below compare actual burglary counts, our Negative Binomial model predictions, and the KDE baseline predictions. Visually, we can start to see where each approach captures spatial pattern of burglaries and where it falls short. When looking at the maps and conducting a visual inspection the middle map, Negative binomial, seems to better capture the spatial spread of burglaries better than the Poisson one when comparing it to the baseline KDE map. 

The performance metrics table then gives us numbers to compare. If our model MAE is lower than the KDE MAE, the garbage cart features added predictive value beyond just knowing where past burglaries happened. If KDE is better, it would suggest the added complexity of the model was not justified by the predictors we chose. Despite the NB map better capturing burglaries, the KDE model does better with MAE and RMSE. While NB was still helpful for showing statistically signficant relationshipos between garbage complaints and burglaries, knowing preivous burglary locations seem to be a stronger predictor.

The error maps above show where the model was most wrong. Blue cells indicate the model underpredicted - actual burglaries were higher than what the model expected, meaning those areas have more crime than our garbage cart predictors would suggest. Red cells are where the model overpredicted. White or near-white cells are where the model was relatively accurate. The maps show a scattered mix of red and blue meaning that the errors appear to be random. However, there are obnvious areas that are red, which are underprecited areas along the west side. The map on the right displays the most errors even going up to 30  in some areas in the south and west parts of Chicago, while the rest of the area shows a dark colour indicting these areas was more reliable there. 

The coefficient table from the final Negative Binomial model shows each predictor as a rate ratio. A rate ratio above 1 means that variable is positively associated with more burglaries, while a rate ratio below 1 means the opposite. All predictors with statistically significant p-values (below 0.05) are contributing meaningfully to the model's predictions. We can see that countGarbage has a rate ratio of 1.007, meaning each additional garbage cart complaint in a cell is associated with a 0.7% increase in expected burglaries. Alhtough this is  statistically significant, it is also a very marginal effect garbage.nn has a rate ratio of 0.997, meaning each additional unit of distance from garbage cart complaints is associated with a 0.3% decrease in expected burglaries. 

## Final Notes and Critical Evaluation

This analysis has several important limitations. First, crime data only reflects reported crimes and policing patterns, where areas with heavier police presence tend to have more recorded crime, which can create a feedback loop in any predictive model. If the model is then used to direct more policing to those same areas, the data bias gets reinforced rather than corrected. This is a core critique of predictive policing that came up in course discussions. Further, even though garbage cart complaints serve as a reasonable proxy for neighbourhood crimes  (burglaries) under broken windows theory, they are  a 311 reporting metric. In other words,  they reflect who calls 311 as much as they reflect actual crimes. Wealthier and more civically engaged neighbourhoods could  have higher 311 usage, which could introduce bias into the predictor.

The model only uses three predictor variables, and there are clearly other factors, like income, housing density, etc., that likely influence burglary risk and are not captured here. The error maps do show some areas of  underprediction, particularly along the west side where the model consistently predicted fewer burglaries than actually occurred, and several cells in the south with absolute errors above 30. 

That said, the analysis does demonstrate spatial relationship between garbage cart complaint hotspots and burglary counts in Chicago. All three predictors were statistically significant, and the directions of the relationships made theoretical sense: more complaints associated with more burglaries, and greater distance from it was associated with less However, the KDE baseline actually outperformed the Negative Binomial model on both MAE (1.92 vs 2.08) and RMSE (2.81 vs 3.13), which is an important finding to sit with honestly. It suggests that knowing where burglaries has occurred is a stronger predictor of future burglaries than knowing where garbage cart  is concentrated.
